passage: When Ms Iyer called Varun to read aloud from the English reader, he stood with the book close to his face and started blinking fast, again and again. From the next bench Nitin whispered, “He didn't even look at it last night, see how his eyes are going.” Ms Iyer heard. “Blinking doesn't tell us that, Nitin. Many people blink more when they're nervous or tired.” She turned back. “Take your time, Varun.” Varun took a breath, put a finger under the line and read on more slowly. By the third sentence the blinking had eased.

qa.q: Who whispered about Varun's eyes?
qa.a: Nitin whispered about them.

qa.q: What might Varun have been feeling while he blinked, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: Most likely nervous about reading in front of the class, since it eased once he slowed down and put a finger under the line. Tiredness can also make people blink more.

qa.q: What did Ms Iyer do that helped?
qa.a: She told the class that blinking does not show what Nitin claimed, and she gave Varun time, which let him settle. 🙂

qa.q: How might Nitin see it after Ms Iyer's words?
qa.a: He may realise he jumped to a conclusion from a cue with many causes, and perhaps feel a little embarrassed.

grounding: A child blinks a lot when nervous reading aloud, which a classmate reads as not having prepared.

passage:
“Read your poem for me, Vishal.”
“Okay.” Vishal held the notebook and blinked, blink, blink, blink.
“Why are you blinking so much?” said Usha. “Did you copy it?”
“No! I wrote it.”
“Your eyes are going like a butterfly.”
Vishal rubbed them. “I'm nervous. And they're tired from the screen lesson.”
Usha put the notebook down. “I'm sorry. I shouldn't decide from your eyes. Read slowly, I'm listening.”
He read. The poem was about a crow in the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Vishal's poem about?
qa.a: It was about a crow in the monsoon.

qa.q: What was Vishal probably feeling when he said “No! I wrote it”?
qa.a: Hurt and nervous about being doubted, since he right away explained the blinking as nerves and tired eyes. He may also have felt worried his poem would not be liked.

qa.q: What did Usha do that repaired the moment?
qa.a: She apologised, stopped judging by his eyes and listened, which let him read without extra pressure.

qa.q: What would change if Usha had kept believing he copied?
qa.a: Vishal might feel distrusted and be even more nervous next time, and the poem would go unheard.

grounding: A child blinks from nerves and tiredness; blinking is not evidence of dishonesty.

passage: I'm Jahnavi. Last summer, when Nirmala Mausi's blue cup broke, she asked me if I'd touched it. I hadn't. But my eyes started blinking fast, blink-blink-blink, and I couldn't stop them. “See, your eyes are telling me,” she said. My throat closed up. I had been reading on the tablet for two hours, so my eyes were already dry and stinging, and then I was scared on top of that. Later the cat was found on the shelf, next to the pieces. Mausi hugged me and said, “Blinking isn't a lie detector. I'm sorry.” I still blink when I'm nervous. Now I know that's all it means.

qa.q: Where was the cat found?
qa.a: The cat was found on the shelf, next to the pieces.

qa.q: What was Jahnavi feeling while blinking fast?
qa.a: Jahnavi felt scared of being blamed, on top of eyes already dry from two hours on the tablet, so the blinking came from nerves and tiredness, not guilt.

qa.q: What went wrong in Mausi's first reading, and what fixed it?
qa.a: She treated blinking as proof of lying; finding the cat, saying sorry and accepting that blinking isn't a lie detector fixed it.

qa.q: How might Nirmala Mausi feel after the cat was found?
qa.a: She probably felt guilty and sorry for doubting Jahnavi only because of blinking.

grounding: Shows a child's nervous, screen-tired blinking being mistaken for lying, and the adult learning it is not evidence of dishonesty.

passage: Reading-group note, Thursday. Nikita, Class 3 teacher. Chaitanya blinked constantly while reading aloud today, sometimes six or seven blinks on one line. Mr Rao, who covered my class on Monday, wrote that Chaitanya “doesn't focus and seems shifty.” I don't agree. When he reads to me alone, the blinking nearly stops. In front of the group it starts again, and his voice speeds up. He also told me his eyes feel scratchy after screen time at home. For now he will read to a partner, and I've asked his parents to get his eyes checked if the scratchiness keeps going.

qa.q: When does Chaitanya's blinking nearly stop?
qa.a: The blinking nearly stops when he reads to Nikita alone.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's blinking in front of the group most likely show?
qa.a: It most likely shows he feels nervous reading to an audience, with scratchy eyes after screen time adding to it, rather than a lack of focus.

qa.q: What two steps did Nikita take, and why do they fit?
qa.a: Nikita let him read to a partner to ease the nerves and asked his parents to get his eyes checked if the scratchiness keeps going, covering both likely causes.

qa.q: Why might Mr Rao read the blinking differently?
qa.a: Mr Rao saw Chaitanya only briefly and may believe blinking means shifty or unfocused, without seeing him read calmly alone.

grounding: Shows a child's frequent blinking while reading aloud being read as shiftiness, when nerves and dry eyes explain it better.

passage: Tuesday night. Dear diary, it's me, Nazia. Today at lunch I told Ankita I'd finished the whole mystery book. She squinted at me. “You're blinking loads. You're lying.” I WASN'T. My eyes have been itchy since swimming yesterday, and then she stared, and I got nervous, and they blinked even more. I said, “Ask me the ending, then.” I told her the ending. She went quiet and said, “Okay, sorry, my cousin says blinking means lying.” I said her cousin should get itchy eyes one day. We laughed. But it felt bad for a minute, being called a liar because of my eyelids 😔

qa.q: Why had Nazia's eyes been itchy?
qa.a: Nazia's eyes had been itchy since swimming yesterday.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when Ankita called the blinking lying?
qa.a: Nazia felt nervous and hurt at being called a liar, and the nerves made the itchy eyes blink even more.

qa.q: What worked in how Nazia answered?
qa.a: Offering to tell the ending gave real evidence instead of arguing about blinking, and it cleared things up calmly.

qa.q: Where did Ankita's idea come from, and how might she feel now?
qa.a: Ankita got it from her cousin, and after hearing the ending she probably felt a bit embarrassed for the accusation.

grounding: Shows a child's nervous blinking, worsened by itchy eyes, being mistaken for lying by a friend, and evidence clearing it up.

passage:
The clay water pot outside the village school lay in pieces, and Hansa had been the last one near it.

"Did you knock it over?" asked Disha Madam.
"No, Madam." Hansa blinked, fast and hard, again and again.
"See, she's blinking. She's lying," whispered Bhola.

Disha Madam didn't answer him. She had seen Hansa blink like that every time she read aloud, and the dust storm that morning had left everyone's eyes red. "Blinking tells me you're nervous, Hansa, not what happened," she said. Then she asked the others. The tea-stall owner across the road had seen it: a grazing goat had butted the pot. Hansa's blinking slowed.

qa.q: What had knocked over the water pot?
qa.a: A grazing goat had butted the pot.

qa.q: What was Hansa most likely feeling as she blinked fast and hard?
qa.a: Nervous at being questioned about the broken pot. Her eyes may also have been sore from the dust storm, so the blinking showed stress or dust, not lying.

qa.q: Which choice was fair, and why?
qa.a: Disha Madam refused to treat blinking as proof and asked others who had seen, which found the real cause.

qa.q: How did Bhola read Hansa's blinking, and why was that unfair?
qa.a: Bhola took the blinking as a sign of lying, but blinking can come from nerves or dust, so it was no evidence at all.

grounding: It shows a child blinking a lot when nervous, a classmate reading it as lying, and a teacher treating it as nerves and checking the facts instead.
